title: Excavation of belowground objects by Dirhinus giffardii (Hymenoptera: Chalcididae)
content:
Abstract
When hosts occur belowground, as do pupae of tephritid flies, the pupal parasitoid Dirhinus giffardii (Silvestri) (Hymenoptera: Chalcididae) sometimes excavates them. This study investigated excavation behavior using the oriental fruit fly Bactrocera dorsalis (Hendel) (Diptera: Tephritidae) as the host. Particular attention was given to the excavation of empty puparia reported previously. Under the host-quality assessment (HQA) hypothesis, empty puparia are excavated because parasitoids cannot reliably distinguish them from viable hosts underground. This explanation was tested by providing viable hosts and empty puparia simultaneously in peat moss at a depth at which parasitism occurred but excavation did not. Parasitoids parasitized only viable hosts and never empty puparia, indicating that they can distinguish between them without excavation and that the HQA hypothesis alone cannot fully explain the behavior. As a complementary proximate explanation, this study proposes the modal action pattern (MAP) hypothesis, under which excavation is probabilistically released by a sign stimulus regardless of the true identity of the object. Consistent with this hypothesis, parasitoids excavated artificial objects made of polystyrene, wood, and stainless steel. Repeated exposure to empty puparia did not detectably reduce excavation. Parasitoids also excavated previously parasitized pupae, although it remains unclear whether excavation can follow oviposition within the same encounter. These results suggest that excavation may be released probabilistically while a sign stimulus is perceived, independently of whether host assessment has already been completed. Excavation by D. giffardii therefore appears to involve a stimulus-driven proximate mechanism consistent with the MAP hypothesis.
